name: Bianca Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and run an injection press making stackable storage bins. My vocational certificate covered mould temperature and safe stops, but a bad lid still needs my hand and eye. I like getting the first lid to snap flush; scraping plastic from a blocked feed is the miserable part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are home and AI use like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works school-kitchen hours. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved. The press wage is low for this job and there are few similar plants nearby. I use AI every day to translate machine manuals and explain alarms, then check the answer against the panel before I touch anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the line crew a chatbot can explain an alarm, but it cannot pull a warped lid off a hot mould. The shop still needs people at the press, and a little office time saved should mean less rushing for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm paid below the usual press-operator rate and our savings cover less than a month. My partner works school-kitchen hours, and we have two children and a mortgage. Even without a new robot, one bad month could put us behind; there are few similar plants nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep running the storage-bin injection press and checking the first lid of each batch. I use AI daily to translate short manual passages, and I'll keep that up, but I verify an alarm code with the maintenance lead before touching the mould. I'll bring the cracked-lid log to our next union branch meeting about paid inspection time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin money margin, even in the quiet picture. A lid has to fit before anyone can call a batch finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the chatbot give you a bad lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday the chatbot translated a fault note as 'coolant low', but the actual machine panel showed a heater fault. I stopped the press and asked the maintenance lead before resetting it. A translated alarm is a clue, not permission to open a hot mould.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home in a tight month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I pay the mortgage right after payday; the school-kitchen wage covers food and bus tickets. There isn't a spare month's income sitting somewhere else. When the children need shoes, we check every other bill twice.

say: A **chatbot** can explain press alarms but cannot remove warped lids safely.
Paid **inspection time** matters more to our crew than a faster office list.
think: Our **low pay** and less than one month saved make ordinary bills tense.
Few **nearby plants** leave little room if a quiet month still goes wrong.
do: **Keep** running the bin press and checking first lids each batch.
**Bring** the cracked-lid log to the union branch meeting about paid inspection time.
feel: **Anxious** about the existing mortgage and thin savings.
S0.quote: A translated alarm is a clue, not permission to open a hot mould.
fieldNote: Bianca **uses AI daily** for manuals but verifies hazards against the machine and maintenance lead.
Her **union meeting** concerns paid inspection time amid low pay and a thin household cushion.

steps.text: Keep running bin press and inspect first lids
Bring cracked-lid log to union branch meeting on paid checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can sort orders and write shift sheets, but slower robots still leave us handling hot plastic. I'll tell our union branch that a new target needs paid training and enough inspection time, not a longer queue of bins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn new screens quickly; I already use AI every day. What scares me is management treating that speed as a reason to cut the press crew or unpaid checking time. Our mortgage has no spare month to absorb shorter shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At Tuesday's branch meeting I'll ask the rep to put paid screen training and first-lid time into the next talks. If the plant offers an actual paid place on the new press-control course, I'll take it; I'll practise the safety stop with the trainer before using any new target. I'll also ask the lead for the posted shift plan before choosing overtime or child care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, although I'm curious about the controls. I can learn a screen faster than I can replace a week's missing pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that course worth attending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The press-control course needs a real trainer and a stopped mould, not just a login to watch at home. I'd practise a false-temperature alarm and a failed safety gate before running production. Paid time is essential because our cushion is so small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the roster changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the roster cuts my regular shifts, I'll ask the branch rep to challenge it with the last three pay slips. The children need the school pickup covered, so a promised extra shift at midnight won't solve the household gap.

say: **Order software** may change schedules before robots take over hot press work.
The union should demand **paid training** and first-lid time with any new target.
think: I can learn **new controls** quickly because I already use AI daily.
A shortened **press roster** could threaten our mortgage before we could adjust.
do: **Ask** union branch to negotiate paid training and first-lid checks.
**Attend** offered paid press-control training with a trainer and stopped mould.
**Check** the posted roster against child pickup and regular pay.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours despite interest in the new controls.
S1.quote: I can learn a screen faster than I can replace a week's missing pay.
fieldNote: She pairs **curiosity** about controls with specific paid safety instruction.
The **union request** concerns real paid hours and inspection time, not a promise of future advancement.

steps.text: Raise paid press training and inspection time at union branch
Attend press-control course if paid trainer-led place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the press crew that thinking AI in 2028 could plan the orders, and capable robots around 2031 could load and inspect the bins. We should meet as a branch now and bargain over wages and notice before the first robot comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the robots can do the hands-on press work. I might lose most of my low-paid hours, and less than a month saved will not carry a mortgage. My partner's school-kitchen hours are not a second full wage. I lie awake thinking which bill gets missed first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll call a union branch meeting this month and ask for a written bargain on notice, pay and funded paid retraining. At home we'll cancel the streaming subscriptions and put the money toward the mortgage. If the plant posts a funded paid place on guarded robot inspection, I'll enrol; after qualifying, if my shifts are cut, I'll apply for posted local inspection work only if the duties are safe and the regular pay and school pickup hours work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The children need reliable press wages every week, and I can't promise them if robots take my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the branch meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the last three pay slips beside the mortgage bill at the meeting. The gap is already narrow, so a few lost shifts would show up before a course certificate did. I want the notice and paid course terms in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would inspection work really last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inspection job needs a real local posting and a base rate that covers the mortgage without counting overtime. If the robot can run the inspection too, I won't pretend the certificate alone protects the job. I would still apply where a human inspector is actually hired.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes orders before capable robots reach our press around 2031.
Our **union branch** should bargain for notice, wages and funded paid training now.
think: At **48**, I could lose press hours while our savings cover under a month.
My partner’s **school-kitchen wage** cannot carry the mortgage alone.
do: **Convene** the branch to seek written notice and paid training terms.
**Cancel** streaming and direct the money to mortgage bills.
**Enrol** if funded paid guarded training offered; apply to safe posted inspection work if qualified and shifts cut.
feel: **Alarmed** about a likely major wage loss and sleepless mortgage worry.
S2.quote: The children need reliable press wages every week, and I can't promise them if robots take my shift.
fieldNote: Bianca expects **major hour loss** from capable robots and names missed bills and lost sleep.
Her **training and application** remain separate, conditional on offered places, qualification, real local posts and workable pay.

steps.text: Call union branch meeting for written notice and paid training terms
Cancel streaming subscriptions to cover mortgage bills
Enrol in guarded robot inspection if funded paid place offered
Apply for posted safe local inspection if qualified, shifts cut, pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years lets us bargain while the press still earns money. Thinking AI in 2031 may schedule our bins first; capable robots around 2034 could take the loading. I want the union to ask for paid training seats before anyone loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when physical robots arrive. Five years could give me a certificate and a little more savings, but only if my regular shifts keep coming. The low wage and mortgage still pinch us today, so I cannot simply pay tuition upfront.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay on the press and put a set amount from any extra paid shift into a new emergency pot after the mortgage. I'll ask our branch rep to negotiate a paid robot-cell maintenance course with fees covered and a real hands-on place. If offered, I'll enrol; once qualified, if hours fall, I'll apply for posted local maintenance roles only where the guard training, regular pay and school-hour travel work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years gives me a calendar. I can check each course and each wage instead of buying a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the practical test include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practical test should make me lock out the press, trace a jam and measure a rejected bin lid. A certificate without that stopped-machine practice would not make me safe beside a robot. I would ask the trainer to sign each task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a maintenance vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need the posted base rate and the shift start before sending an application. One plant across town wants a dawn start that clashes with the children's school run. A vacancy on paper is useful only if we can actually work it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 could plan the bin orders, and capable robots around 2039 could run the press floor. A decade is time to argue for who gets the savings, but people on low wages need the first year of help now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when hands-on robots can do my job. The children will be older, though I cannot assume the mortgage is gone. A technical diploma might open a maintenance role, but the tuition and evening hours have to fit this family before I call it a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the technical college for the exact timetable and employer sponsorship terms this winter. If a funded evening diploma place opens with paid practical time on guarded equipment, I'll enrol; after qualifying, if my press shifts shrink, I'll apply for posted local maintenance jobs with safe duties and enough regular base pay. I'll also keep going to branch meetings so our pay terms are heard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the later robots and still worried by this month's bills. Ten years gives room for learning, but it does not make a low wage into a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would evening study fit at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner covers the school kitchen until midafternoon. An evening class cannot begin before I collect the children unless we pay for care, and we don't have that money now. I would need the actual offered place and schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at the branch meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that a diploma does not pay the mortgage by itself. The posted maintenance wage and safe shift must exist where we live. If those jobs vanish too, the union should still bargain for notice and income support.

Low-paid crews need **near-term support** while bargaining over later machine savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture frightens me most because capable robots around 2031 could take the press hours before we have money to bridge even a month. Written notice, a funded paid safety course and a real posted local job at enough base pay would help. I'd want our branch in the room when those terms are set.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs off a plastic bin lid after a robot clears a jam. A customer should not have to discover a cracked rim because the line chased a number.

headlineQuote: A customer should not have to discover a cracked rim because the line chased a number.
portrait: **Bianca**, 43, is a mid-level injection-press operator with a vocational certificate and daily AI use for manuals.
She and her school-kitchen partner support **two children** and a mortgage with under a month saved.
Her **progressive outlook** turns pay and safety concerns into actual union branch meetings, while she stays curious about controls.
Fast robots make her **alarmed** about lost low-paid hours; funded practical learning and real local vacancies shape her response.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable press robots around 2031 before the family can bridge a lost wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded paid safety training and a posted safe local job with enough base pay would help.
